summary: An informational memo written to calm worries that sending options in a TFTP request might make servers that do not understand options misbehave. It analyzes how such servers would react to the extended request and concludes the option scheme is safe to use. It specifies no standard.

eli5.summary: Before asking a shop for something new, you check that a clerk who has never heard of it will just say no and not get confused. This memo shows that is what happens.

questions: is tftp option negotiation safe for old servers
what happens when a tftp server does not support options
is tftp option negotiation backward compatible
what happens when an old tftp server receives option data
how does backward compatibility work in tftp
subtitle: Testing backward compatibility of TFTP option negotiation with old servers.

tldr.problem: A new option negotiation scheme for TFTP was proposed, but implementers worried that old TFTP servers would misbehave if sent option information they did not understand.
tldr.mechanism: Malkin and Harkin tested a modified TFTP client sending option negotiation packets against five unmodified TFTP servers from different vendors, and examined the BSD TFTP code that spawned many implementations. In every case, old servers ignored the option information and proceeded normally.
tldr.outcome: The analysis confirms that TFTP option negotiation is fully backward compatible with unmodified servers. Servers that do not understand options simply ignore the extra data and process the transfer as before.

facts.label: Result
facts.value: All servers ignored options and completed normally

today: RFC 1785 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It documents the analysis that paved the way for TFTP option extensions (RFC 1782, RFC 1783, RFC 1784) to be deployed safely. The backward-compatibility finding has held in practice as these extensions have been widely adopted.

sections.title: TFTP Option Negotiation
sections.content:
TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a simple file transfer protocol defined in RFC 1350. A new extension, proposed in RFC 1782, adds option negotiation: a way to negotiate parameters like blocksize before the transfer begins.

The option mechanism is backward compatible by design. However, implementers worried that sending options to an old server—one that predates the option extension—might cause unexpected behavior. This memo documents tests to verify the concern was unfounded.
sections.eli5: TFTP is a simple way to copy files. Engineers wanted to add a way to ask for special features, but worried old photocopiers might break if you asked for something they did not understand.

sections.title: Testing Old Servers
sections.content:
A TFTP client was modified to send option negotiation in its request packets and tested against five unmodified TFTP server implementations on different systems: DEC Alpha running OSF1, SGI MIPS running IRIX, Sun SPARC running SunOS 5.1, IBM RS/6000 running AIX, and another Sun running SunOS 4.1.3.

In every case, the servers ignored the option information and processed the transfer as though no option negotiation had been attempted. The transfer succeeded.

In addition, the authors examined the BSD 4.3 TFTP source code, the foundation for many implementations. The code clearly ignores any extraneous data in request packets, confirming that the protocol design was sound.
sections.eli5: They sent a new kind of request to five different old photocopiers. All five just ignored the new stuff and copied normally. They also looked at the original code: yep, it is set to ignore anything it does not recognize.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility Confirmed
sections.content:
The test results demonstrate that the TFTP option negotiation mechanism is fully backward compatible with unmodified TFTP servers. Servers that do not understand option negotiation simply ignore the extra data and proceed with the standard transfer protocol.

This means implementers can safely deploy option negotiation extensions without breaking compatibility with existing deployed TFTP servers. The results give confidence that the design of the negotiation mechanism—to include options in the request packet without changing the basic structure—achieves its goal of graceful degradation.
sections.eli5: It is safe to roll out the new feature. Old photocopiers will just say "I do not get it" silently and copy anyway.
